subject: biology
title: Ecosystems, populations and succession
key_idea: An ecosystem is a community of organisms together with the non-living parts of its environment. Each species has a niche, and its population is limited by biotic and abiotic factors up to a carrying capacity. Over time, succession changes a community until it reaches a stable climax.

blocks.text: This section defines the levels of organisation in an ecosystem. Ecosystems are dynamic: they change over time and vary hugely in size.

items.meaning: All the organisms of one species living in the same place at the same time.
All the populations of different species living in the same place at the same time.
The place where a population lives, with its own conditions.
A community and the non-living (abiotic) components of its environment, interacting together.
The role of a species in its ecosystem: how it fits in with its biotic and abiotic surroundings.

items: Ecosystems range from very small (a rock pool, a rotting log) to very large (a woodland, an ocean).
A playing field and a large tree are ecosystems of different sizes.
Ecosystems are **dynamic**: their conditions and populations change over time.
Populations form a community; a community plus its abiotic environment forms an ecosystem.
A habitat is where a species lives; a niche is what it does and how it fits in.

blocks.text: Each species is adapted to a particular niche. Its niche is set by both abiotic and biotic conditions, and so explains where it lives and how many there are.

diagram.alt: Sort factors into abiotic and biotic.
diagram.prompt: Sort each factor into the correct group.

items: **Abiotic factors** are the non-living conditions, such as temperature, light, pH, water and wind.
**Biotic factors** come from other living organisms, such as food supply, predation, disease and competition.
A species is found where the abiotic conditions suit its adaptations and its biotic needs are met.
Two species cannot occupy exactly the same niche in the same habitat. If they try, one is out-competed.
Abiotic factors are non-living; biotic factors come from other organisms.
A species' niche explains its distribution (where it lives) and its abundance (how many there are).

blocks.text: An ecosystem can support only a certain size of population of a species. This is called the carrying capacity.

items.meaning: The maximum population size of a species that an environment can support.
A factor in short supply that stops a population growing any larger.

items: **Abiotic factors** such as light, temperature, water and mineral ions limit population size. A drought or a cold winter lowers it.
**Intraspecific competition** is between members of the same species, for food, space, mates or light. It becomes stronger as the population grows.
**Interspecific competition** is between different species that share resources. The better-adapted species can reduce the population of the other.
**Predation** reduces the prey population, and the number of prey affects the number of predators.

blocks.text: Predator and prey numbers rise and fall in linked cycles. When prey are plentiful, predators increase. More predators then reduce the prey, so predators later decline.

items: The prey peak comes before the predator peak.
The predator population falls when food runs short, which lets the prey recover.
Abiotic factors affect both populations too, so the cycle is not perfectly regular.
Population size varies around the carrying capacity set by limiting factors.
Competition (within and between species) and predation control numbers alongside abiotic factors.

blocks.text: Succession is the gradual change in the species of a community over time. Primary succession starts on bare ground that has never had soil, such as new rock, sand dunes or lava.

diagram.alt: The stages of primary succession in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the stages of primary succession in order.
steps: Pioneer species such as lichens and mosses colonise bare rock
Pioneers die and decay, forming a thin soil
Small plants such as grasses and ferns grow in the soil
Shrubs and larger plants take over as soil deepens
Trees grow and shade out smaller plants
A stable climax community is reached

items: **Pioneer species** are the first to colonise. They tolerate harsh conditions and often fix nitrogen or photosynthesise.
At each stage the organisms change the abiotic environment: soil forms, deepens and holds more water and minerals.
The environment becomes less hostile, so new species with different adaptations can survive and biodiversity increases.
The new species can make conditions unsuitable for the earlier species, which are out-competed and replaced.

blocks.text: The final stage is the **climax community**. It is stable, with a balance of species that depends on the climate, such as woodland in the UK.

items: **Deflected succession** happens when human activity stops succession at one stage, so a different community results. Mowing a lawn or grazing keeps grassland and prevents woodland.
The stopped community is a **plagioclimax**.
Conservation often manages succession, for example by grazing or cutting heathland to keep a habitat from turning into woodland.
Primary succession runs from pioneer species to a stable climax community, with each stage changing the environment.
Human activity can deflect succession, and conservation often manages it.

checks.q: Distinguish between a habitat and a niche.
checks.a: A habitat is the place where an organism lives. A niche is the role of the species in the ecosystem, including how it is adapted to its biotic and abiotic conditions.

checks.q: Explain how intraspecific competition helps to keep a population near its carrying capacity.
checks.a: As the population grows, resources such as food and space become scarcer. Competition becomes stronger, so fewer survive and reproduce, and the population falls. When it falls, competition lessens and the population can rise again.

checks.q: Describe how pioneer species allow primary succession to continue towards a climax community.
checks.a: Pioneers colonise bare ground and change the abiotic environment. When they die and decay, they form soil that holds water and minerals. Conditions become less hostile, so new species with different adaptations can grow, out-compete the pioneers and increase biodiversity until a stable climax community forms.

items: Conservation of habitats often involves managing succession.
You should be able to discuss the conflict between human needs and conservation, to keep natural resources sustainable.
You should evaluate evidence and data about conserving species and habitats, including conflicting evidence.
Investigate the effect of a named environmental factor on the distribution of a given species, for example light on the distribution of a plant.
Know examples of ecosystems of different sizes, such as a rock pool, a playing field and a large tree.
Name examples of biotic and abiotic factors for each.
Know deflected succession, where succession is stopped by human activity, and give an example.
